newsitem.title: USA: Hayes eyes Micronics in comeback strategy.
newsitem.headline: Hayes eyes Micronics in comeback strategy.

text.p: Hayes Microcomputer Products Inc.'s merger talks with Micronics Computers Inc. are part of a strategy to take Hayes public and give the modem maker a war chest for acquisitions, Hayes Chairman Dennis Hayes said.

Hayes said a Micronics merger would be one step in a comeback plan that includes additional acquisitions, new high-speed products and aggressive marketing of the modem industry's most famous brand name.

"We will develop the company through internal growth that fills in the product line and through acquisition," he said in an interview on Wednesday. "It has been part of our plan to go public via the shortest path possible."

The effort to merge with Micronics by the No. 2 modem maker is known on Wall Street as a reverse buyout, in which a company goes public by merging with another company whose shares are already publicly traded. Hayes could then use its stock to acquire other companies, chiefly rival modem makers.
Hayes declined to comment on the status of negotiations with Fremont, Calif.-based Micronics, a maker of motherboards -- the internal chassis of a personal computer.
But sources close to the talks said the two companies are haggling over the exchange ratio of the stock swap that would lead to a merger. The talks were disclosed by Micronics in a statement June 13.

Founded in 1977, Norcross, Ga.-based Hayes pioneered the consumer modem during the early days of the PC and came to dominate the market in its first decade of business. Modems let computers communicate over phone lines, allowing users to hook up to online services and the Internet.

But over the years Hayes' leadership was undercut by lower-cost competitors. It fell into Chapter 11 bankruptcy in 1994 and emerged in April 1996 with the help of outside investors from Singapore, led by Acma Ltd., and from Hong Kong, led by affiliates of Shenzhen Kaifa Technology Ltd. and Wong's International (Holdings) Ltd.
Dennis Hayes continues to own about half of the company.
Hayes is a distant second in market share for modems, trailing 3Com Corp.'s U.S. Robotics Corp., according to research firm Dataquest. Robotics had about 22 percent and Hayes about 8 percent.
Other name players in the modem business include Boca Research Inc., Diamond Multimedia Systems Inc. and Zoom Telephonics Inc.
Asked whether Hayes and Micronics had discussed a succession, Hayes would only say he had no plans to retire and no plans to move the company from its Norcross headquarters.
Sources close to Hayes said the founder planned to remain in charge of a merged Hayes-Micronics company, which would be renamed Hayes Communications Inc.

Once publicly traded, Hayes plans to embark on a new round of acquisitions of U.S. and overseas modem suppliers, similar to its purchase in March of Cardinal Technologies Inc. from Microsoft Corp. co-founder Paul Allen's Vulcan Ventures.
Financial terms of that acquisition were not disclosed.
Of Cardinal's 100 employees, Hayes kept six sales staff members and 10 other people. Hayes, with 800 employees, shifted Cardinal modem production to its own plants.
The combination of Hayes' brand name and its long-running development expertise with Micronics' capabilities promises to cut manufacturing costs and make Hayes more competitive.
Micronics' motherboards, when combined with Hayes chipsets, would allow Hayes modems to be built directly into new PCs. Hayes sells all its modems as stand-alone products.

Micronics is an attractive acquisition target because the net value of its assets is near its current share price, sources close to Hayes said. Micronics stock rose 6 cents to $2.875 in afternoon trading on Nasdaq Thursday.
In 1996 Hayes had $260 million in revenues and a net loss of $1 million, compared with 1995's $8 million loss. Officials said they expect the company to turn a profit in 1997.
